name: Goff, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the petition to transfer should be granted.

name: Loretta H. Rush Chief Justice
description: Concurred, argued that Ward's claims regarding the method of execution do not challenge the validity of his conviction or sentence and thus are not appropriate for successive post-conviction relief.

name: Goff, J.
description: Concurred in part, arguing that Ward failed to show the execution chamber's soundproofing and one-way glass violate his constitutional rights; Dissented in part, arguing the court should set an execution date only after Ward's public records requests regarding the lethal injection protocol are resolved to allow him to raise constitutional issues effectively.

name: Chief Justice Rush
description: Concurred, argued that timely appeals of temporary civil commitments generally do not become moot when the commitment ends due to potential collateral consequences, and that sufficient evidence supported J.F.'s commitment.

name: Justice Slaughter
description: Concurred in part and in the judgment, argued that the case is not moot and sufficient evidence supports the commitment, but dissented from the Court's embrace of the 'public interest' exception to mootness, advocating for a 'capable-of-repetition' exception consistent with separation of powers, and emphasized the judiciary's independent duty to ensure cases remain live controversies.

name: Loretta H. Rush
description: Dissented, argued that the warrantless search of Jackson's trunk violated his constitutional rights under Article 1, Section 11, and that the Court should have granted transfer to address this important issue.

name: Molter, J.
description: Dissented, joined Chief Justice Rush's opinion that the warrantless search of Jackson's trunk violated his constitutional rights.

name: Shepard, Senior Judge
description: Concurred, argued that the court granted rehearing and modified the opinion by striking "biological" from the phrase "biological division of being either female or male" while reaffirming the original decision in all other respects.

name: SLAUGHTER, JUSTICE.
description: Concurred, argued that at the directed-verdict stage, courts can review the reasonableness of inferences from evidence but cannot weigh conflicting evidence or assess witness credibility, as this would infringe on the constitutional right to a jury trial.

name: Molter, Justice
description: Concurred, argued that the law is constitutional as it predominantly furthers public policy objectives, does not unconstitutionally take property, and does not impair contracts.

name: Goff, Justice
description: Concurred, argued that the Indiana Constitution guarantees the right to a jury trial in civil forfeiture cases, as historical records and legal analogy show it is an action at law, not equity.

name: Justice Goff
description: Concurred, argued that the Indiana Constitution protects the right to a jury trial for in rem civil forfeitures, which are essentially legal actions, not equitable disgorgement.

name: Goff, Justice
description: Concurred, argued that while the jury determines habitual offender status, only evidence proving or disproving prior convictions is relevant, and Harris's testimony about his circumstances was irrelevant.

name: Justice Molter
description: Concurred, argued that Harris's testimony was irrelevant based on existing evidentiary rules, making constitutional analysis unnecessary to resolve the appeal.

name: Justice Massa
description: Concurred with Justice Molter's opinion, arguing that the trial court properly excluded Harris's proffered evidence as irrelevant.

name: Chief Justice Rush
description: Dissented, argued that the jury's constitutional right to determine habitual offender status includes considering evidence beyond just prior convictions, and Harris's testimony about his primary felony was relevant.

name: Justice Slaughter
description: Dissented, agreed with Chief Justice Rush's proposed disposition for Harris but preferred to avoid addressing constitutional questions when possible.

name: Rush, Chief Justice
description: Concurred, arguing that HEA-1123 is unconstitutional because it violates the fixed-by-law requirement for legislative sessions and infringes on the Governor's exclusive authority to call special sessions, thereby violating the separation of powers.

name: Justice Massa
description: Concurred, argued that the statute is constitutional under Article 1, Section 9 of the Indiana Constitution because the expressive activity constituted an "abuse" and the statute serves public health, welfare, and safety. Also argued the statute is constitutional under the First Amendment because it serves a compelling government interest (privacy) and is narrowly tailored, surviving strict scrutiny.

name: Massa, Justice
description: Concurred, argued that Bloomington merely defined fraternities and sororities based on their relationship with IU, which was a permissible legislative judgment and not an improper delegation of authority, thus finding no constitutional violations.
